*   **Vertex File:** Binary file containing vertex positions $(x, y, z)$ and scalar field values.
*   **Tetrahedra File:** Binary file containing tetrahedron definitions.
In the normalized state, each record contains the actual vertex values (positions and scalars) for all 4 vertices, rather than indices.
*   **Intersection File:** Binary file containing records of ray-cell intersections.
*   Interpolated scalar field value for lighting (float).
If the input uses an indexed format (vertices with coordinates/scalars, tetrahedra with integer indices), the data must be dereferenced to create the normalized files.
Create two binary files: one for vertices, one for tetrahedra (initially with indices).
*   Externally sort the tetrahedra file by the $k$-th vertex index using external mergesort.
*   Perform a synchronous scan of the vertex file and the sorted tetrahedra file.
Since the tetrahedra are sorted by vertex index, the corresponding vertex data can be retrieved sequentially.
Output the dereferenced position and scalar field values into a new temporary tetrahedra file.
Replace the original tetrahedra file with the new file.
*   Read each tetrahedron from the normalized file sequentially.
*   Transform the tetrahedron vertices using the specified transformation matrix.
*   Compute ray intersections for all pixels in the screen resolution.
*   Write a record $(\rho_i, z_0, z_1, s)$ to the Intersection File, where $s$ is the interpolated scalar field value for lighting.
*   Sort the Intersection File using an external sort algorithm.
*   The comparison function sorts primarily by Pixel ID $p_i$ (ascending), and secondarily by depth $z$ (ascending).
*   Traverse the sorted Intersection File sequentially.
*   For each pixel, accumulate the samples in the order they appear (which is front-to-back).
*   Apply transfer functions to light and composite the samples.
*   **Precision:** Floating-point precision in depth sorting must be sufficient to maintain correct front-to-back ordering, especially for thin cells or grazing rays.
*   **Disk I/O:** The performance is heavily dependent on disk I/O speed.
*   **Memory Usage:** The algorithm assumes a constant, small amount of RAM.
If the system runs out of memory for the external sort buffers, the sort will fail or degrade significantly.
*   **Unstructured Grids:** This method is specifically designed for unstructured grids (tetrahedra).

The rendering phase involves one pass over the geometry ($O(t \cdot \text{rays})$), one external sort ($O(N \log N)$ where $N$ is the number of intersections), and one pass over the sorted intersections ($O(N)$).
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(1)$ with respect to the dataset size.
*   **When to use:** When rendering very large unstructured volumetric datasets on systems with severe memory constraints.
*   **When not to use:** When rendering speed is critical, or when sufficient memory is available for in-core techniques.
